chunks.text: 2 Method We consider a sequential multi-domain scenario in which biomarker domains { D 1 , … , D K } \{D_{1},\dots,D_{K}\} are introduced progressively. At training step t t , only data from the current domain D t D_{t} are accessible, while previous data are unavailable. After training on D t − 1 D_{t-1} , the generator is frozen as a teacher model G t − 1 G^{t-1} , serving as a stable reference. During adaptation to D t D_{t} , the student model G t G^{t} is optimized using current-domain supervision together with a structural preservation objective computed against G t − 1 G^{t-1} on previous domains. Unlike replay-based methods, we preserve knowledge via cross-biomarker structural relations. The fourth domain process is used for illustration. 2.1 Base Multi-domain Virtual IHC Framework We build our framework upon Adaptive Supervised PatchNCE (ASP), an encoder–decoder generative model for H&E-to-IHC translation trained with adversarial and patch-level contrastive supervision. Given an H&E image x x and a biomarker domain index d ∈ { 1 , … , K } d\in\{1,\dots,K\} , the generator produces a stain-specific output: y ^ d = G ​ ( x , d ) \hat{y}_{d}=G(x,d) (1) In our setting, domain indices correspond to different biomarkers (e.g., 1 1 : HER2, 2 2 : ER, 3 3 : PR, 4 4 : Ki67). Bottleneck-only domain injection preserves domain-invariant morphology and confines biomarker-specific modulation to a compact latent space by applying feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM) [ 16 ] at the bottleneck, where the domain index is encoded as a one-hot vector 𝐞 d \mathbf{e}_{d} and mapped to an embedding 𝐮 d = ψ ​ ( 𝐞 d ) \mathbf{u}_{d}=\psi(\mathbf{e}_{d}) . Let 𝐡 b \mathbf{h}_{b} denote the bottleneck feature following [ 12 ] .

FiLM modulates it as: 𝐡 b ′ = ( 1 + 𝜸 b ​ ( d ) ) ⊙ 𝐡 b + 𝜷 b ​ ( d ) \mathbf{h}_{b}^{\prime}=(1+\boldsymbol{\gamma}_{b}(d))\odot\mathbf{h}_{b}+\boldsymbol{\beta}_{b}(d) (2) where [ 𝜸 b ​ ( d ) , 𝜷 b ​ ( d ) ] = ϕ b ​ ( 𝐮 d ) [\boldsymbol{\gamma}_{b}(d),\boldsymbol{\beta}_{b}(d)]=\phi_{b}(\mathbf{u}_{d}) . This builds a lightweight unified conditional virtual IHC backbone for continual cross-domain relation preservation. 2.2 Domain-Aware MoE Extractor for Relational Modeling A key challenge in continual multi-domain virtual staining is representation interference : as the generator adapts to a new biomarker domain, the latent representations of previously learned domains are implicitly reshaped. Such interference destabilizes cross-domain structural relations, making relation preservation difficult to enforce. To address this issue, we construct a domain-aware feature extractor F MoE F_{\mathrm{MoE}} that produces structured and disentangled representations for different biomarker domains. Patch Sampling and Shared Projection: For each biomarker domain d ∈ 𝒟 d\in\mathcal{D} , we extract intermediate encoder features { 𝐟 ℓ , d } ℓ ∈ ℒ \{\mathbf{f}_{\ell,d}\}_{\ell\in\mathcal{L}} , where 𝐟 ℓ , d ∈ ℝ B × N ℓ × C ℓ \mathbf{f}_{\ell,d}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times N_{\ell}\times C_{\ell}} denotes patch-level tokens at layer ℓ \ell ( N ℓ N_{\ell} is the number of spatial tokens). We randomly sample P P spatial tokens to obtain a compact set of structural descriptors, which are then projected into a shared embedding space: 𝐨 ℓ , d = Sample ​ ( 𝐟 ℓ , d ) ∈ ℝ B × P × C ℓ , 𝐳 ℓ , d = ϕ ℓ ​ ( 𝐨 ℓ , d ) ∈ ℝ B × P × C ℓ \mathbf{o}_{\ell,d}=\mathrm{Sample}(\mathbf{f}_{\ell,d})\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times P\times C_{\ell}},\quad\mathbf{z}_{\ell,d}=\phi_{\ell}(\mathbf{o}_{\ell,d})\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times P\times C_{\ell}} (3) where ϕ ℓ \phi_{\ell} is a two-layer MLP applied to each token independently.

The projection function is shared across domains to align patch-level representations in a unified latent space. This shared space is designed to emphasize morphology-related structures rather than biomarker-specific appearance, enabling meaningful cross-domain relational comparison. Domain-Aware Mixture-of-Experts Modeling: To explicitly incorporate domain structure while preserving content awareness, we introduce a domain-aware mixture-of-experts module. The biomarker domain d d is encoded as a one-hot vector 𝐞 d \mathbf{e}_{d} and mapped to a compact embedding 𝐮 d = ψ ​ ( 𝐞 d ) \mathbf{u}_{d}=\psi(\mathbf{e}_{d}) . Importantly, the expert routing is conditioned on both the domain embedding and the image content representation. We denote the gating network by 𝒢 gate \mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{gate}} , which corresponds to the 𝒢 gate \mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{gate}} block shown in Fig. 2 . For each token embedding 𝐳 ℓ , d \mathbf{z}_{\ell,d} , the gating network 𝒢 gate \mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{gate}} predicts domain- and content-adaptive expert weights: 𝐰 ℓ = softmax ​ ( g ℓ ​ ( [ 𝐳 ℓ , d , 𝐮 d ] ) ) \mathbf{w}_{\ell}=\mathrm{softmax}\Big(g_{\ell}([\mathbf{z}_{\ell,d},\mathbf{u}_{d}])\Big) (4) where M M experts { h ℓ , m } m = 1 M \{h_{\ell,m}\}_{m=1}^{M} produce the domain-aware structured feature: 𝐅 ℓ , d = Normalize ​ ( ∑ m = 1 M 𝐰 ℓ , m ⊙ h ℓ , m ​ ( 𝐳 ℓ , d ) ) {\mathbf{F}}_{\ell,d}=\mathrm{Normalize}\!\left(\sum_{m=1}^{M}\mathbf{w}_{\ell,m}\odot h_{\ell,m}(\mathbf{z}_{\ell,d})\right) (5) This domain-aware structured feature space reduces cross-domain interference and provides a stable basis for relation preservation. MoE Regularization.

The training set includes 4,642, 4,361, 4,153, and 4,139 pairs for HER2, Ki67, ER, and PR, respectively, with 1,000 testing pairs for each biomarker.

The availability of multiple biomarker domains derived from whole-slide images enables systematic evaluation of continual multi-domain virtual IHC staining. Implementation Details: We adopt ASP [ 10 ] as the backbone for virtual staining. All continual learning baselines are implemented on the same ASP framework, differing only in the adopted continual learning strategy. All input H&E–IHC patches are resized to 512 × 512 512\times 512 . In the continual multi-domain setting, biomarker domains are learned sequentially without accessing samples from previously learned domains. Unless otherwise specified, each domain is trained for 50 epochs with a batch size of 1 on a single NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU. The learning rate is set to 1 × 10 − 4 1\times 10^{-4} using the Adam optimizer. Evaluations: We assess image quality using PSNR [ 1 ] and SSIM [ 19 ] , and distribution-level similarity via FID [ 7 ] . To better capture histopathology-specific features, we report CONCH-FID [ 2 ] using a pathology-pretrained CONCH encoder [ 14 ] , which captures pathology-aware semantic similarities through pathology image-text contrastive pretraining and provides a more clinically relevant assessment of staining quality, and DISTS [ 4 ] for structural and textural perceptual consistency. To mitigate representation interference and structural drift, we propose ContiStain, a domain-aware relational distillation framework with structured MoE features and cross-domain structural consistency. Experiments on the four-domain MIST show it effectively reduces forgetting while maintaining structural coherence, suggesting that preserving latent cross-domain relations is a practical mechanism for scalable and robust continual virtual staining under real clinical constraints.
